plain.0: The first five chapters argued that there is an ultimate cause behind everything. This chapter asks what that cause must be like, and whether the five arguments all point to the same thing. To answer, Feser first sets out some general rules of reasoning, then uses them to work out God’s characteristics one by one.
plain.1: A basic rule: a cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. But “have” can mean three things. I can give you $20 because I have the bill, because I have the money in the bank, or because I can print the bill myself. The cause doesn’t need to look like the effect; it just needs the resources to produce it.
plain.2: A critic says the rule is obviously false: a sponge cake is spongy, but eggs, flour, and butter aren’t. Feser answers that the critic forgot the rest of the cause — the baker, the mixing, the oven. The ingredients don’t need to be spongy; the whole process just needs the power to make sponginess.
plain.3: Even philosophers who reject God use this rule. Some argue that because humans come from purely physical causes, humans must be purely physical — which assumes the rule. And evolution doesn’t break it: genes, mutations, and the environment together produce each new trait.
plain.4: What a thing does depends on what it is. Plants grow because they’re alive; rocks don’t, because they aren’t. Nothing can do, all by itself, something beyond its own nature — though something else can make it do so, the way a puppeteer makes a puppet dance.
plain.5: This rule isn’t just old church philosophy. A famous argument that the soul survives death uses it, and so does a well-known non-religious philosopher, John Searle, when he criticizes a certain theory of the mind. The point is that many thinkers rely on the rule, whatever they believe about God.
plain.6: We use words in three ways. Sometimes a word means exactly the same thing twice (“Fido is a dog,” “Rover is a dog”). Sometimes it means totally different things (a baseball bat versus a flying bat). And sometimes it means related but not identical things (“good wine,” “a good person”). That last way, called analogy, is still literal — and even the word “exists” works like that.
plain.7: There are different kinds of analogy. Sometimes a word really applies to one thing and to others only because of their connection to it: food is “healthy” because it makes people healthy. Sometimes it really applies to each thing in its own way: plants and animals are both truly alive. And sometimes it’s just a figure of speech: calling a brave man “a lion.”
plain.8: “Being” — the idea of existing — isn’t a category like “animal” that splits into subtypes, because there’s nothing outside existence to split it with. Instead, things exist in ways that are alike in pattern but different in detail, the way seeing a tree and “seeing” a math answer are both real seeing.
plain.9: Feser gives a short argument for this. Both what a thing is and what it could become are real — a sleeping pianist really can play — but they aren’t real in exactly the same way. They aren’t real in totally unrelated ways either. So they are real in related ways, which is what analogy means.
plain.10: This matters for talking about God. If words meant exactly the same for God as for us, God would just be a big version of us. If they meant something totally different, we’d be saying nothing. Analogy is the middle path that lets us say true things about God without shrinking him down to our size.
plain.11: The ultimate cause can have no untapped potential at all — not even in what it does. What a thing does reflects what it is, and a being with both a fully real side and an untapped side would be made of parts, which would need something else to hold them together. Then it wouldn’t be the ultimate cause.
plain.12: How can there ever be two of something? Two coins differ because they’re made of different metal; a penny and a dime differ by some added feature. Either way, you need parts. The ultimate cause has no parts, so there is nothing that could make a second one. There is, and could only be, one God.
plain.13: The five arguments describe the ultimate cause in five ways: fully real, having no parts, existence itself, the mind behind necessary truths, and a being that can’t fail to exist. Feser shows each description implies the others. So the five arguments aren’t pointing to five gods but to one God seen from five angles.
plain.14: Saying God has no parts (“simplicity”) is the key to the whole picture. If God were made of parts, something would have to hold the parts together, and that something would be more basic than God. And God would be just one member of a “god” category — like Zeus being the last god left on Mount Olympus. That wouldn’t be God at all.
plain.15: Some modern religious philosophers reject this and think of God as a person like us, only without limits. The philosopher Alvin Plantinga argued that if God had no parts, God would be just an abstract idea. Feser replies that Plantinga misunderstands the view: our words for God’s power and knowledge are different, but they can describe one undivided reality.
plain.16: Some new truths about you don’t involve any change in you. If your brother grows taller, you become “shorter than your brother” without shrinking. God becoming “Creator” is like that: the world changes by coming into existence, but God doesn’t change. This answers critics who say God must have changeable features.
plain.17: God can’t change: change means gaining something you lacked, and God lacks nothing. But that doesn’t make God inactive or lifeless. Acting just means making something happen, and being alive means acting from within yourself — and nothing acts more fully from itself than God.
plain.18: God isn’t made of matter. Physical things always have parts and can be rearranged, broken down, or changed — even the tiniest particles. Since God has no parts and nothing untapped in him, God can’t be physical, not even some invisible energy or force.
plain.19: God never began and can never end. But more than that, God isn’t in time at all. Being in time means your life keeps adding new moments and you keep changing along with them. God doesn’t change, so God exists outside time rather than just living for an infinitely long time.
plain.20: Critics ask: if God keeps things existing today and tomorrow, isn’t he acting today and tomorrow? Feser says no. Think of an author who dreams up a whole novel at once: inside the story, chapter 10 comes after chapter 1, but the author didn’t think of them one after the other. God creates the whole timeline in a single act from outside it.
plain.21: Some philosophers say “necessary” only applies to word definitions, like “bachelors are unmarried,” so a being can’t exist necessarily. Feser replies that truths like 2 + 2 = 4 are necessary without being about words, and that the arguments for God already explain what makes God’s existence necessary.
plain.22: Another critic says, “I can imagine a world with nothing in it, not even God, so God doesn’t have to exist.” Feser replies that you can’t picture God at all, any more than you can picture the number four itself. And what must be true of a thing is learned from what the thing is — not from what we can imagine.
